content.text: could we improve communqiue's release notes? look at jdx.dev projects and their release notes and how it's doing
I’ll look at the projects on jdx.dev, compare their recent release notes, and check how Communiqué generates them to find concrete improvements.

The notes often explain real user impact well, especially mise’s examples and upgrade details. The recurring weakness is over-explanation: small releases still list internal maintenance, and some bullets read like PR implementation summaries. I’m checking the release workflows and configuration to distinguish Communiqué’s output from other generators.

Yes. **Communiqué is good at explaining changes, but needs stronger editorial judgment about what to include and when to stop.**

I sampled recent releases across the [15 projects on jdx.dev](https://jdx.dev/), inspected release workflows and project configuration, and read Communiqué’s generation code. The sample included 40 published releases; not all use Communiqué.

What’s working:

- **Useful examples and adoption details.** [mise 2026.9.5](https://github.com/jdx/mise/releases/tag/v2026.9.5) explains new configuration with TOML examples, defaults, and required watcher restarts.
- **Clear explanations of bugs.** [pitchfork 2.25.0](https://github.com/jdx/pitchfork/releases/tag/v2.25.0) connects malformed cookie forwarding to broken login sessions.
- **Actionable feature descriptions.** [mise-action 4.3.0](https://github.com/jdx/mise-action/releases/tag/v4.3.0) provides a usable `minimum_release_age` example and explains precedence.

The biggest weaknesses:

| Problem | Observed example | Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| Internal work leaks into notes | [Communiqué 1.3.5](https://github.com/jdx/communique/releases/tag/v1.3.5) says there are no user-facing changes, then explains release-plz, `GH_REPO`, and mbx updates. | For maintenance-only releases, stop after one sentence and the compare link. |
| Bullets become implementation essays | [tak 0.0.10](https://github.com/jdx/tak/releases/tag/v0.0.10) spends most of its release explaining manifest fields and signing mechanics. | Lead with the benefit; retain technical details only when needed to use or upgrade. |
| Minor changes receive disproportionate attention | [hk 1.58.1](https://github.com/jdx/hk/releases/tag/v1.58.1) explains preview-card dimensions, renderer, font, caching, and layout. | “Shared documentation links now show page-specific previews” is enough. |
| Repetition survives the existing guidance | [mr-boxington 1.11.0](https://github.com/jdx/mr-boxington/releases/tag/v1.11.0) repeats display changes through its opening, Highlights, and Added sections. | Give each change one main explanation. |
| Small-release introductions become boilerplate | tak’s three sampled releases all begin “A small release.” | State the actual change immediately; short notes already communicate small scope. |

**The code helps explain why this happens.** The [prompt](/Users/jdx/.codex/worktrees/0c20/communique/src/prompt.rs) already prohibits internal noise and repetition, but also explicitly asks small releases to announce their size. It asks for a “catchy” title and tells the model to match previous releases’ structure. That can perpetuate verbosity and boilerplate. fnox and pitchfork even have project-specific instructions to avoid copying sponsor sections from those references.

I’d prioritize three changes:

1. **Tighten the default editorial instructions.** Concrete titles, direct openings, usually one or two sentences per bullet, and no inventory of omitted maintenance. Preserve examples, compatibility details, and required user actions.
2. **Make style references subordinate to quality rules.** Reuse terminology and formatting without inheriting length, repeated sections, or workflow-appended footers.
3. **Evaluate against real releases.** Use these small, medium, and large releases as a comparison set. Check factual support, omitted important changes, repetition, and usefulness—not just whether the prompt contains the right instructions. Current submission checks cover output structure and links, not editorial quality.

For example, I’d reduce tak’s latest opening and feature description to:

> Release downloads now include a signed manifest that installers can use to verify the archives’ checksums and provenance. The manifest is published as `packslip.sigstore.json` alongside the existing checksums.

My recommendation is to start with the prompt and reference handling, then compare regenerated notes against this sample before adding a separate model review pass.
